html:
ARPANET, the Advanced Research Projects Agency Network, was a US research network of computers that began in 1969 and grew into the internet. It was shut down in 1990, once newer networks had taken its place.

It was paid for by ARPA, a research agency of the US Department of Defense set up in 1958 in response to Sputnik. The idea, pushed by J. C. R. Licklider and then Bob Taylor from 1966, was to let researchers share scarce, expensive computers at distant universities. The project was led by Larry Roberts.

Its key choice was packet switching: messages were broken into small blocks, each sent separately by whatever route was free and put back together at the end. There was no central point that controlled the whole network. The first link joined computers at UCLA and the Stanford Research Institute in October 1969. The first message was meant to be "LOGIN", but the system crashed after "LO".

Milestones:

  • 1971: email between computers on the network, sent by Ray Tomlinson, who chose the @ sign.
  • 1973: the first links abroad, to Norway and Britain.
  • 1974: Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn published TCP/IP, a common language that let different networks connect, forming an "internet".
  • 1983: ARPANET switched to TCP/IP, often seen as the birth of the internet.

In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee in Europe proposed the World Wide Web, which ran on top of the internet and opened it to everyone. Like the telephone a century earlier, ARPANET changed how people communicate.
sum: ARPANET, the Advanced Research Projects Agency Network, was a US research network of computers that began in 1969 and grew into the internet. It was shut down in 1990, once newer networks had taken its place.
